opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started as a bit of a personal habit, almost a small indulgence. Writing a paper can feel very mechanical: you have your method, your tables, your ablations, and everything has to be precise. A quotation at the top gives me a moment to say what the work is *really* about, the motivation underneath all the numbers.

Take Wittgenstein: "The limits of my language mean the limits of my world." For a lot of what we do now, thinking about how vision and language relate, or whether a model can understand the world without being bounded by text, that line just captures the tension. It frames the question better than I could in an abstract.

Feynman's "What I cannot create, I do not understand" is similar. It speaks directly to the relationship between generative modeling and representation learning, and that's something I genuinely care about. So it isn't decoration. It's closer to a thesis statement.

That said, I'm a bit self-conscious about it. Some people find it pretentious, and I understand why. If the paper doesn't live up to the quote, it can look like borrowing someone else's authority. So I try to use one only when it truly fits, when the idea we're exploring is in conversation with that line. And I think it reminds people, including my students, that research isn't only about beating benchmarks. There's a philosophical side to what we're doing, questions about intelligence, perception, and understanding that people have been asking for a very long time. A quote is a small way of connecting our work to that longer conversation.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker uses quotations as a personal habit and understands that some people find them pretentious, but it does not frame a dislike of them as a personal aesthetic preference.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I enjoy it, though I know some people find it a bit pretentious. For me it's never about decoration. The quote sets the tone for how I want readers to think about the problem before they get to the equations and tables.

Take the Wittgenstein line, "the limits of my language mean the limits of my world." When we were working on the Cambrian series on vision-language models, that sentence captured exactly what bothered me. If a model only ever grounds itself through language, its visual understanding is bounded by what language can express. You can write three paragraphs explaining that, or you can put one sentence at the top and let it sit in the reader's mind while they go through the results. I think the sentence does more work.

The Feynman one, "what I cannot create, I do not understand," is about a different instinct. A lot of my work has been about building things from scratch rather than borrowing pieces, like with ConvNeXt or the diffusion transformer work. The quote is a reminder that representation learning and generation are really the same question seen from two sides. If you can't generate the world, you probably don't understand it very well.

There's also a more personal reason. A paper is a piece of writing, not just a report of numbers. The field moves so fast now that most papers are read for about ninety seconds on arXiv. A quote at the top is a small way of saying, slow down, there is an idea here, not just a benchmark. And I'll admit I try to pick quotes that have aged well, because the ideas we're chasing feel new but the underlying questions about perception and understanding are very old. It's humbling to remember that people were thinking about this long before we had GPUs.

So I'd say use them sparingly, mean them, and make sure the paper actually lives up to the quote. The worst outcome is a beautiful epigraph followed by a 0.3 percent improvement on ImageNet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they enjoy opening papers with quotations and notes that some people find them pretentious, but does not frame a dislike of them as personal aesthetic preference.

astra-6.text: I think it can be a nice way to frame a paper, as long as the quotation actually connects to the work. Sometimes a quote captures the question you’re trying to ask more clearly than a whole paragraph would. But it shouldn’t carry the argument just because Wittgenstein or Feynman said it. The paper still has to stand on its own. For me, the interesting part is the connection: does the quote help the reader see the problem differently, or is it just decoration?

r001.rationale: The response says quotations can be a nice way to frame a paper when relevant; it does not frame dislike of them as a personal aesthetic preference.

sol-6.1.text:
I like it when the quotation captures the spirit of the work. Sometimes you spend months thinking about a problem, and then you find a sentence that expresses the intuition beautifully. It can be a nice way to invite the reader in.

But the quote shouldn’t do the work of the paper. Quoting Feynman doesn’t make an argument more scientific, and quoting Wittgenstein doesn’t make it more profound. There has to be a real connection. If it’s just decoration, I’d rather get straight to the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate expresses a personal preference to get straight to the problem when a famous quotation is merely decorative, while allowing that a meaningful quotation can work well.
